possible_reaction_pattern: Itchy or tingling mouth after raw apple is common in birch-pollen-related apple allergy.
plain_explanation: Mal d 1 is an apple protein similar to a birch-pollen protein. Some people allergic to birch pollen react to raw apple because their immune system recognises the similar shape.
possible_cross_reactivity: Bet v 1 in birch pollen; PR-10 proteins in some fruits and vegetables
important_caution: Cooked apple is often, but not always, better tolerated. This app cannot tell you whether a food is safe for you.

possible_reaction_pattern: Can be associated with more widespread reactions in some people, particularly in certain regions.
plain_explanation: Mal d 3 is a tough apple protein called a lipid-transfer protein. It can survive cooking and digestion better than Mal d 1.
possible_cross_reactivity: Other fruit and nut lipid-transfer proteins, especially in Mediterranean regions
important_caution: Reactions involving breathing trouble, faintness, or widespread hives need urgent medical care.

possible_reaction_pattern: May contribute to reactions in people sensitised to pollen profilins.
plain_explanation: Mal d 4 is apple profilin. Similar profilins occur in many pollens and plant foods, so cross-reactivity is possible.
possible_cross_reactivity: Bet v 2 and other pollen profilins
important_caution: A reaction to one plant food does not automatically mean reaction to all plant foods.

possible_reaction_pattern: A major peanut storage protein; may be relevant in peanut allergy.
plain_explanation: Ara h 1 is a large nutrient-storage protein in peanut. It is one of the proteins that the immune system can target in peanut allergy.
possible_cross_reactivity: Other legume and nut cupins, though clinical cross-reactivity varies
important_caution: Peanut allergy can be severe. Do not use this app to decide whether a food is safe.

possible_reaction_pattern: One of the most important peanut allergens and is associated with severe reactions in some people.
plain_explanation: Ara h 2 is a small, stable peanut seed protein. It is a major target of IgE antibodies in many people with peanut allergy.
possible_cross_reactivity: Some tree-nut and seed 2S albumins; clinical relevance varies
important_caution: Even tiny exposures can matter for some people with peanut allergy. Follow an allergist’s advice.

possible_reaction_pattern: A major peanut storage protein that can withstand processing.
plain_explanation: Ara h 3 is another nutrient-storage protein in peanut. It can remain relatively stable during cooking and digestion.
important_caution: Peanut allergy should be assessed by an allergy specialist.

possible_reaction_pattern: Often linked with birch-pollen sensitivity rather than primary peanut allergy.
plain_explanation: Ara h 8 is a peanut protein similar to birch-pollen Bet v 1. Some birch-pollen-allergic people react to it, often with milder mouth symptoms.
possible_cross_reactivity: Bet v 1 in birch pollen; PR-10 proteins in fruits and vegetables
important_caution: A positive test to Ara h 8 does not by itself prove a severe peanut allergy.

possible_reaction_pattern: A peanut lipid-transfer protein; more often important in some southern European populations.
plain_explanation: Ara h 9 is a tough peanut protein that can survive heat and digestion. It may be important for some people with peanut allergy, particularly in certain regions.
possible_cross_reactivity: Other nsLTPs, including peach Pru p 3
important_caution: Geography and individual testing matter; this app cannot predict your reaction.

possible_reaction_pattern: A soybean storage protein involved in some soy allergies.
plain_explanation: Gly m 5 is a large nutrient-storage protein in soybean. It can be a target of the immune response in soy allergy.
possible_cross_reactivity: Other legume storage proteins; clinical cross-reactivity varies
important_caution: Soy allergy and peanut allergy are separate conditions; having one does not automatically mean having the other.

possible_reaction_pattern: A soybean storage protein involved in some soy allergies.
plain_explanation: Gly m 6 is another major nutrient-storage protein in soybean. It can be recognised by IgE antibodies in some people with soy allergy.
important_caution: Processed soy foods vary widely; do not assume a product is safe based on this entry.

allergen: Kunitz trypsin inhibitor / Gly m TI
possible_reaction_pattern: A soybean defence protein that can block protein-digesting enzymes; its allergy role varies.
plain_explanation: This protein helps protect the soybean and can interfere with protein digestion. Some people with soy allergy may react to it, but it is not the only or always the main soy allergen.
important_caution: This entry is educational; protease inhibitors are not a reliable marker of soy allergy on their own.

possible_reaction_pattern: A major shrimp allergen that can cause food allergy and may relate to dust-mite sensitivity.
plain_explanation: Pen m 1 is a muscle protein in shrimp. People allergic to it may also react to other shellfish because similar proteins occur across shellfish.
possible_cross_reactivity: Other shellfish tropomyosins; dust-mite and cockroach tropomyosins
important_caution: Shellfish allergy can be severe. Cross-reactivity is common but not universal.

possible_reaction_pattern: Major milk proteins involved in cow’s-milk allergy.
plain_explanation: Caseins are the main proteins in cow’s milk. In milk allergy, the immune system can react to one or more of these proteins.
possible_cross_reactivity: Goat and sheep milk caseins; cross-reactivity is common
important_caution: Baked-milk tolerance is individual and should only be assessed with medical guidance.

possible_reaction_pattern: A heat-stable egg-white protein often important in egg allergy.
plain_explanation: Ovomucoid is an egg-white protein that can remain relatively stable during cooking. It is often important in persistent egg allergy.
possible_cross_reactivity: Eggs from related birds may cross-react
important_caution: Do not trial baked egg without advice from an allergist or clinician.

possible_reaction_pattern: The most abundant egg-white protein and a common egg-allergy target.
plain_explanation: Ovalbumin is the main protein in egg white. It is often affected by heating, which is why some people tolerate baked egg better than loose egg.
important_caution: Tolerance to one egg product does not prove tolerance to all egg products.

possible_reaction_pattern: A major birch-pollen allergen that can lead to reactions to certain raw fruits and vegetables.
plain_explanation: Bet v 1 is a birch-pollen protein. Some people sensitised to it develop itching in the mouth after eating foods with similar PR-10 proteins, such as raw apple.
possible_cross_reactivity: Mal d 1 in apple; Ara h 8 in peanut; PR-10 proteins in other plant foods
important_caution: Pollen-food reactions are individual; this app cannot diagnose them.
